Pacific sand lance (Ammodytes personatus) embryos develop within a discrete chorion until hatching is triggered by the activation of chorionase. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 19.1 °C [T = 19.1 °C], the incubation period from fertilisation to larval eclosion lasts 32 days [ab = 32 days], a duration that aligns with the relatively slow developmental rates observed in cold-water Ammodytidae. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before mouth opening occurs, has an initial wet weight of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams]. This minute mass, calculated from the average egg diameter reported for the congener Ammodytes marinus, underscores the species' extreme altriciality at the onset of the planktonic larval phase. Following yolk-sac resorption and the transition to exogenous feeding, the actively growing larva enters a pelagic stage characterised by rapid somatic growth and morphological differentiation.

As the planktonic larva approaches metamorphosis, a pronounced allometric shift in body proportions occurs, culminating in benthic settlement and the acquisition of a juvenile body plan. Field surveys of post-settlement young-of-year indicate that puberty, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and gonadal recrudescence, is attained at a standard length of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds closely to the maturation schedules of other sand lance species inhabiting comparable high-latitude environments. At this pubertal stage, the wet weight of the individual averages 8.3 grams [Wwp = 8.3 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial accumulation of somatic tissue during the juvenile growth phase. Once sexually mature, the reproductively active adult continues to grow asymptotically, approaching an ultimate standard length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] under favourable feeding conditions.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for this species, based on length-weight regressions developed from field-caught specimens, is 62.9 grams [Wwi = 62.9 grams]. This asymptotic mass represents the upper bound of somatic growth, which is typically approached after several years of feeding on calanoid copepods and other lipid-rich zooplankton in nearshore foraging grounds. In comparison to the mass at puberty, the threefold increase between 8.3 grams and the ultimate wet weight highlights the considerable post-maturational growth that characterises this iteroparous teleost. A gravid female near this asymptotic size can direct considerable resources toward reproduction, producing numerous batches of demersal adhesive eggs over a single spawning season when water temperatures are appropriately elevated. The size-based fecundity relationship, derived from volumetric estimates of ovary contents, suggests that reproductive output scales steeply with female length.

Under thermal conditions typical of the species' southern spawning aggregations, where surface waters reach 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], each female achieves a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 43.6 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 43.6 offspring per day]. This high daily fecundity reflects the combined effect of a large clutch size and the ability to spawn repeatedly at short intervals during the peak of the breeding season. The daily rate was estimated from the allometric scaling of fecundity with adult length, and it positions the Pacific sand lance among the more prolific members of its family. Spawning events typically occur over sandy substrates in shallow coastal waters, where the adhesive eggs adhere to sand grains and develop in situ until hatching. The synchrony of spawning with spring phytoplankton blooms ensures that first-feeding larvae encounter abundant prey immediately following yolk-sac resorption.

Longevity records compiled from otolith-based age determinations of wild-caught individuals indicate that the maximum lifespan of Pacific sand lance is 4.5 years [am = 4.5 years] when development occurs at 19.1 °C [T = 19.1 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, typical of small-bodied, fast-growing forage fish, is balanced by the species' high reproductive output and early maturation. The combination of a 32-day embryonic period, a pubertal length of 8 centimeters, and a maximum longevity just under five years positions A. personatus as a quintessential r-selected strategist within its temperate marine ecosystem. Natural mortality is elevated during the planktonic larval phase due to predation by gelatinous zooplankton and larger piscivores, but survivors that recruit to the benthic juvenile stage face lower predation pressure. The species' life history thus reflects a trade-off between rapid maturation and high fecundity on one hand, and a comparatively brief reproductive window on the other.
